title: The History of Railroad Trestles — Why America Built 200-Foot Bridges Entirely From Wood
fullText: In 1868, a passenger train crept across a wooden bridge in southeastern Wyoming at 4 mph. The bridge was 700 ft long and sat 150 ft above a creek so small you could [music] step across it. The whole structure swayed in the wind. Engineers refused to stay in the locomotive cab. They would hand the controls to the firemen, climb down [music] and walk beside the train rather than ride across. This was the Dale Creek Bridge on the Union Pacific Railroad, and it was considered one of the greatest engineering achievements in America. It was also built entirely from wood, and it terrified [music] almost everyone who crossed it. But this bridge was not unusual. Across the United States in the second half of the 1800s, railroad companies built hundreds of massive wooden bridges, some of them towering over 200 ft above canyon floors, stretching a/4 mile [music] from one cliff face to another. They were called trestles, and for about 50 years, they were the backbone of American rail expansion. They carried freight trains loaded with ore, passenger cars packed [music] with families heading west and logging equipment into some of the most rugged terrain on the continent. And then almost all of them disappeared. The story of how America came to build these enormous structures from nothing but timber and why they [music] eventually abandoned every single one starts with something that seems obvious but actually set the United States [music] apart from every other industrialized nation on Earth. Wood. Lots of it. In Europe, railroad bridges were built from stone and iron because that is what engineers there had always used. Stone arch bridges had been around since the Roman Empire, and European countries had centuries of masonry tradition to draw from. When railroads arrived in England and France in the 1830s, engineers naturally built with the materials and techniques they knew best. America was different. [music] The continent was covered in forests. Old growth timber stretched from the Appalachian [music] to the Pacific coast, and it was staggeringly cheap. A railroad company could send a crew into the nearest stand of trees, cut what they needed, drag the logs to [music] the construction site, and have a bridge framed up in weeks. Try that with stone, and you are looking at months of quarrying, shaping, and careful placement. Iron was available, but it was expensive to manufacture and had to be shipped long distances in a country [music] that was still building its industrial base. So, American engineers made a practical decision. They would build with wood. It was fast. It was cheap. And it was everywhere. This was not laziness or corner cutting. It was a deliberate strategy. Get the railroad open for business as quickly as possible. Start earning revenue from freight and passengers and then use that money to replace the wooden bridges with [music] permanent iron or stone structures later. The attitude was simple. Fix it up and improve it later and pay for it with the earnings. That quote [music] comes straight from the railroaders themselves and it defined how America built its entire rail network. The wooden trestle bridge was in many ways a purely American invention. [music] Trestles in their basic form had been around since Leonardo da Vinci sketched rigid frame designs in the 1500s. But the massive timber railroad trestle, the kind that stood 20 stories above a river gorge and carried a locomotive across, that was born in the United States starting around 1840. And it never really caught on in Europe because Europeans simply did not have the same combination of endless forests and urgent need to move fast. And urgency is really the key word here. Because the event that turned timber trestles from a practical solution into a national obsession was the race to build the transcontinental railroad. On July 1st, 1862, in the middle of the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln signed [music] the Pacific Railroad Act. The law authorized two companies to build a railroad connecting the Missouri River to the Pacific Ocean. The Central Pacific Railroad would start in Sacramento, California, and build eastward. The Union Pacific Railroad would start near the [music] Iowa Nebraska border and build westward. Wherever they met, the line would be complete. The government sweetened the [music] deal with an incentive structure that practically begged for reckless speed. For every mile of track laid on flat ground, each company [music] would receive $16,000 in government bonds. For track through foothills, that jumped to 32,000. and for every mile through the mountains, $48,000 per mile. On top of that, the companies received land grants of 6,400 acres for every 10 mi of track. By the time the railroad was done, [music] the two companies controlled roughly 180 million acres of land. That is about the size of Texas. With that kind of [music] money on the table, both companies had one overriding priority. lay track as fast as humanly possible. Every mile meant more bonds, more land, more wealth, and that meant building bridges at a pace that would have horrified a European engineer. It also meant cutting corners. Both companies built shoddy bridges and flimsy sections of track that they knew would need to be rebuilt later just to claim the mileage first. At one point, the two railroads were building parallel [music] grades right past each other because neither wanted to stop and neither had been told exactly where to meet. Congress [music] eventually had to step in and order them to connect at Promonary Summit in Utah [music] where the famous Golden Spike was driven on May 10th, 1869. The Central Pacific faced the Sierra Nevada mountains almost immediately out of Sacramento. [music] Chinese laborers, roughly 13,000 of them, became the backbone of the mountain [music] construction crews. They blasted tunnels through granite using black powder and nitroglycerin, sometimes consuming 500 kegs of explosive per day. And where tunnels could not be cut fast enough, they built massive wooden trestles along the steep western slopes of the [music] mountains. These trestles hugged cliff faces thousands of feet above river valleys, allowing the track to snake through terrain that would have otherwise been impossible. One trestle near Cape Horn on the Central Pacific line stretched, 1100 ft long along a cliff face above the American River. Workers, both Chinese and white, were suspended by ropes while they hacked, drilled, and blasted a ledge from the sheer granite slope 2500 ft above the rushing water below. The trestle they built there [music] was meant to be temporary, a way to get trains moving while a more permanent solution was engineered. But temporary in the railroad business often meant decades. Over on the Union Pacific side, the workforce was primarily Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans who had spent the war rebuilding railroad bridges that Confederate forces destroyed. And that Civil War experience [music] actually mattered more than you might think. During the war, the United States military [music] railroad had controlled over 2,000 mi of track, and Confederate raiders made a habit of burning bridges [music] to disrupt Union supply lines. Military engineers got very, very good at throwing up replacement trestle bridges in [music] record time. One famous example was a 780 ft long, four tiered railroad trestle [music] built by the first Michigan engineers in Tennessee in 1864. It looked like it [music] could barely hold a man, let alone a supply train, but it held. Abraham Lincoln himself once [music] described a similar wartime bridge over the PTOAC as being built of bean poles and cornstalks. When those same engineers and veterans went west after the war, they brought that battlefield mentality with them. The attitude was get it built, get the trains rolling, [music] worry about permanence later. And nowhere was that attitude more dramatically tested than at Dale Creek in Wyoming. Dale Creek itself was almost a joke. It was about 2 feet wide and a foot deep, a tiny stream that you could [music] literally hop over without getting your boots wet. But the gorge had carved through the granite [music] over thousands of years was not a joke at all. The railroad needed to cross that gorge at the highest point [music] on the entire Union Pacific line near Sherman Summit at over 8,000 ft of elevation. The bridge they built was 720 ft long and [music] 150 ft tall. It was completed in April of 1868 using timber hauled to the site from surrounding forests. An article in [music] Nebraska's Omaha Herald called it a miracle of modern engineering, [music] describing it as a pine timber bridge, jointed, cross- tied, intertwined, self-supporting, and perfectly secure. Perfectly secure was, to [music] put it gently, optimistic. When the first train crossed on April 23rd, 1868, the whole bridge swayed in the Wyoming [music] wind, not a gentle flex. A visible stomachdropping sway that made passengers grip their [music] armrests and prey. Carpenters were rushed to the site to shore up the structure, and in the scramble, two of them fell to their deaths from the bridge. The Union Pacific's chief engineer on the ground, Samuel Reed, watched the bridge move [music] and realized immediately that the design engineers back east had not accounted for the ferocity of Wyoming [music] wind. He ordered ropes tied from the bridge to the canyon walls as emergency stabilizers. Those ropes were replaced with steel cables as soon as they could be shipped in. Even after the reinforcements, [music] trains were required to slow to 4 mph when crossing. The concern was not really about the bridge collapsing [music] under the weight. It was about the wind literally blowing empty box [music] cars off the rails and into the gorge below. A passenger crossing in 1873 [music] wrote that the trestle bridge looks like a light, frail thing to bear so great weight. But fears are not expressed because of the frail appearance of the bridge, but in regard to the tempest of wind, so fierce that we fear the cars may [music] be blown from the track. In the providence of God, she wrote, the wind decreased. Some locomotive [music] engineers flat out refused to ride in the cab across Dale Creek. They would hand the controls to the firemen, climb down from the locomotive, and walk across [music] the bridge on foot, then hop back on the train once it reached solid [music] ground on the other side. On at least one occasion, a group of cowboys who [music] had been drinking decided to ride their horses across the bridge just for the thrill of it. Whether they made it across sober is not [music] recorded. The wooden Dale Creek Bridge lasted until 1876 when it [music] was replaced by an iron structure built on the same peers. Even the iron version was considered dangerous because of the wind and the entire crossing was eventually abandoned in [music] 1901 when the Union Pacific rerouted the line 3 mi south to a lower [music] elevation with less exposure to storms. Now, the Dale Creek Bridge was dramatic, [music] but to really understand how insane timber trestle construction got in America, you need to look at the logging railroads of the Pacific Northwest. This is where the tallest, most jaw-dropping wooden bridges in history were built, and nearly every single one of them is gone today. Starting in the late 1800s, logging companies in Washington State, Oregon, and British Columbia needed railroads to get timber [music] out of the mountains. The terrain was brutal. Steep slopes, deep canyons, and dense forest everywhere you looked. The solution was to build narrow gauge railroad lines that snaked across mountain sides, following the contour of the land. And wherever the tracks needed to cross a valley or [music] ravine, up went a wooden trestle. These were not modest bridges. Montana's two Medicine Creek trestle on the Great Northern Railway stood 214 ft tall. The Cedar River logging trestle in Washington State was a 203 ft high wall of wood that looked less like [music] a bridge and more like a wooden skyscraper lying on its side. and a timber trestle over the crooked river gorge in central Oregon sat nearly 320 ft above the water, taller [music] than the Statue of Liberty. The construction process for these giants was terrifying in itself. Timber trestles came in two basic forms. The simpler version was the pile trestle where crews used pile drivers to pound wooden poles straight into the ground, spacing them 12 to 16 ft apart. Each group of poles was [music] called a bent. and a bend typically consisted of three to five round timber poles arranged with the center post vertical and the outer posts angled slightly outward [music] for stability. For taller bridges, engineers used framed bents. These were built [music] from squared timbers and constructed in stories, each story standing between 10 and 50 ft tall. For extremely high trestles, each section was assembled flat on the ground as a single or double story, then lifted by [music] an aerial high line, stretched across the canyon and lowered onto the growing [music] structure. Workers would repeat this process story by story, building the bridge from the ground up like [music] stacking wooden blocks, except each block weighed several tons, and one wrong move meant [music] a fatal fall. The how Truss design patented in the 1840s by Thomas and Caleb Pratt was the standard template for railroad bridges. What made the how Truss clever was that it [music] combined wood with iron. The main structural members were timber, but the vertical tension members were iron rods. This mattered [music] because green unseasoned wood shrinks and warps as it dries, which would normally cause a wooden bridge to become [music] dangerously loose over time. The iron rods in a how truss could be tightened to compensate for wood shrinkage, allowing builders [music] to use whatever lumber was available without waiting months for it to season properly. Speed again was the priority. For the logging railroads, the trestles were never meant to last. The whole business model depended on moving fast. A logging company would survey a mountainside, build a web of railroad tracks along the contour [music] lines, extract all the marketable timber, and then abandon the tracks, and move on to the next mountain. The trestles they left behind would simply rot and collapse into the canyons they once spanned. None of the dozen or so tallest timber bridges ever built [music] still exist. Nearly half of these 200 ft monsters were constructed for logging railroads in Washington state and on Vancouver Island in British Columbia. [music] They were built to serve a temporary purpose and once that purpose was fulfilled, they were left to the elements. But the most ambitious timber trestle project in American history was not built in the mountains at all. It was built across a lake. In 1902, the Southern Pacific Railroad began construction on what would become known [music] as the Lucin Cutoff, a 102mm railroad line across the Great Salt [music] Lake in Utah. The original transcontinental route went around the north end of the lake through the Promonary Mountains. But [music] that route included brutal grades that required expensive helper engines to push trains over [music] the summit. Edward Henry Haramman, who had taken control of the Southern Pacific in 1901, decided it was time for a shortcut. The shortcut involved building 12 m of wooden trestle directly across the open water of the Great Salt Lake. When Haramman first proposed the idea, [music] plenty of people thought he had lost his mind. Building a railroad trestle across a lake with an unpredictable salt [music] and mud bottom where water depths varied wildly, and no one was entirely sure the lake floor could support the weight of a [music] bridge seemed like a recipe for disaster. Haramman did it anyway. 3,000 men went to work under Chief Engineer William Hood, and they worked 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Electric lights were strung across the Great Salt Lake so construction could continue through the night. Special pile drivers were built that could hammer timber piles into the lake bottom. Gas- powered boats were shipped in from San Francisco to ferry materials. 500,000 gallons of fresh water were hauled in daily from Death, Nevada just to supply the steam engines, pile drivers, and construction equipment. The numbers from this project are staggering. 38,000 trees were cut down for the trestle, the equivalent of a two square mile forest. 400 side dump railroad cars hauled nearly 8 million cubic yards of dirt and stone for grading. The Finnish trestle was 16 ft wide, 12 mi long, [music] and it carried trains directly across the middle of the Great Salt Lake. By 1904, [music] the Lucen Cutoff was operational. It eliminated 44 mi of extreme grades and curves from the old route, saving the Southern Pacific 20 hours of transit time and up to $60,000 per month in operating costs. By 1908, five passenger trains and seven freight trains [music] were crossing the trestle every day in each direction. There was even a train station called Mid Lake sitting on a platform in the middle of the Great Salt Lake, which is exactly as surreal as it sounds. The Lucen Cutoff trestle lasted until the late 1950s when it was replaced by a solid fill causeway built alongside it. That causeway effectively split the Great Salt Lake into two halves with different salinity levels, creating an environmental [music] consequence that nobody in 1904 could have predicted. The old trestle timbers were eventually salvaged [music] in the 1990s by a company that reclaimed the Douglas fur and redwood for use in furniture, flooring, and decorative woodwork. The salt water had pickled the wood over decades, giving it a [music] unique coloring that became a selling point. A bridge built to move trains became a source of [music] luxury lumber a century later. For all their ingenuity, timber trestles had serious problems that ultimately ended their era. The most obvious was fire. Locomotives in the 1800s burned wood or coal, and they threw sparks. A lot of sparks. Running a fireb breathing steam engine across a bridge made entirely of dry timber was in hindsight [music] an obvious disaster waiting to happen and it happened regularly. The great bridge over the American River at Sacramento, a how trust structure that was over a mile long, including its trestle approaches, burned down just a few years after it was built. Rot was the second killer. Untreated wood exposed to rain, snow, and seasonal temperature changes lasted about 20 years before it deteriorated to the point of being dangerous. Timber that sat in water rotted even faster. Railroad companies that intended to replace their wooden bridges with permanent structures often found that the bridges decayed before they got around to the replacement, [music] forcing emergency rebuilds that ate into the profits the bridges were supposed to generate. Collapse was the third problem, though it was less common than popular imagination suggests. The bridges looked terrifying. All spindly legs and exposed frameworks swaying in the breeze, [music] but most of them held up remarkably well under normal conditions. The real danger came when conditions were not normal. Floods, avalanches, and high winds could all bring a trestle down. [music] In 1903, an avalanche in the northern Pacific Mountains swept away part of a trestle [music] that stood 300 ft tall and had been carrying trains since 1890. The wreckage was spectacular on logging railroads where maintenance [music] budgets were slim and bridges were considered disposable. Collapse was [music] a more regular occurrence. There are numerous accounts of train crews who would routinely hop off their slowm moving locomotive [music] as it approached a particularly suspect trestle, let the engine cross on its own, then run across the bridge on foot and jump back on once [music] it reached the other side. That was not an emergency procedure. That was just Tuesday on a logging railroad. By the early 20th century, the writing was on the wall for timber trestles. Steel had become cheaper and more widely available. Concrete technology was advancing rapidly, and railroad companies were running heavier, faster trains that demanded stronger bridges. The old wooden trestles [music] that had been built as temporary stop gaps were now genuine bottlenecks, forcing trains to slow to a crawl on routes where speed meant money. The transition was not instant. It played out over decades. Some wooden trestles [music] were replaced with steel bridges built on the same foundations. Others were simply filled in with dirt and rock dumped between the trestle legs until the whole canyon was packed solid and the wooden structure was buried alive inside its own replacement. This filling process was actually the most common fate for timber trestles on mainline railroads. The trestle was built first to get trains running, then gradually filled with earth hauled in by those same trains until eventually the wooden bridge was no [music] longer needed because it was encased in a man-made hillside. A few timber trestles survived into the modern era through a combination of remote location, low traffic, and sheer stubbornness. The most famous survivor is the Goat Canyon Trestle in the Ciso Gorge of San Diego County, California. The railroad it belongs to was called the Impossible Railroad when it was completed in 1919, connecting San Diego with the Imperial Valley [music] through some of the most punishing desert terrain in the country. Engineers said the route could not be built. The terrain [music] was too steep, too unstable, and too remote. They built it anyway. Then one of the tunnels [music] collapsed. Rather than try to bore through the mountain again, engineers decided to build a wooden trestle that would carry the tracks around the collapsed tunnel and through the open canyon. Built in 1933, well after steel had become the standard material, the Goat Canyon trestle was constructed from wood specifically because the extreme temperature fluctuations in the desert canyon could have caused metal fatigue in a steel bridge. The redwood timber they used handled the heat and cold better [music] than steel would have. The Goat Canyon trestle is 600 ft long and roughly 200 ft tall. Built with a 14° curve to resist the canyon's [music] notorious high winds. It was assembled without nails using only bolts and gravity. A fire suppression tank car was stationed near one of the adjacent tunnels as a permanent precaution. Today, it is recognized as the largest freestanding wooden trestle in the world. And reaching it requires a brutal hike through remote desert [music] terrain with no shade, no water sources, and almost no trail markers. The difficulty of getting there is probably what has kept [music] it standing. Nobody has bothered to tear it down because hardly anyone can reach it. Looking back at the Timber Trestle era, what stands out is not just the scale of what was built, but the mindset behind it. America in the 1800s was a country that prioritized speed over permanence, ambition over caution, and revenue over durability. The wooden trestle was the perfect expression of [music] that philosophy. It was not elegant. It was not built to last, but it worked, [music] and it worked fast enough to open up a continent. The men who built these bridges. The Chinese laborers dangling from ropes above the American River. The Irish veterans [music] hammering pile bents into frozen Wyoming soil. The logging crews assembling 20story [music] frameworks in the rain soaked forests of Washington state. They were not building monuments. They were building [music] tools. The trestle was a means to an end, a way to get the track across the gap so the trains could start running [music] and the money could start flowing. And the numbers tell the story of what that speed made possible. Before the transcontinental railroad, a trip across the country cost about $1,000 and took months by [music] wagon. After the railroad was completed, the price dropped to $150 and the journey took about a week. Towns along the tracks [music] grew into cities. Farmers could ship crops to distant markets. An entire economy reorganized itself around the iron rails that wooden bridges [music] made possible. The timber trestle was a bridge in both the literal and metaphorical [music] sense. It bridged canyons and rivers, obviously, but it also bridged the gap between what America was [music] and what it was becoming. It was the temporary structure that made the permanent transformation [music] possible. And then, like so many temporary things, it was discarded once it had served its purpose. Today, if you know where to look, you can still find traces of the trestle era. Rotting wooden pilings in river valleys that have not seen a train in a century, concrete and earthfill, embankments with old timber barely visible inside them. the Goat Canyon trestle baking in the California desert sun and furniture made from Douglas fur timbers that spent a hundred years standing in the middle of the Great Salt Lake. The age of the wooden railroad trestle lasted barely 70 years from the 1830s to the early 1900s. In that span, American engineers built some of the tallest, [music] longest, and most audacious wooden structures in human history. And then they replaced [music] almost every single one. The timber trestle was never meant to be remembered. It was meant to be used up. But the country [music] it helped build is still here, still connected by the rail corridors. Those wooden bridges opened up, still moving freight and passengers along routes that were first crossed by trains creeping over swaying walls of wood 200 ft above the canyon floor.
